title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text: MRMhub-viz is a standalone, interactive application for reviewing the peak-integration results produced by INTEGRATOR (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 3). It is distributed as a self-contained executable (~10 MB), resides in the same folder as the MRMhub application, and is launched like any other application. Because it reads the binary results written to the misc/ folder during peak integration, Step 3 must have been run at least once before the visualizer can display a dataset.

title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text:
What it displays
The transition to be inspected is selected from the dropdown menu in the top-left corner. For the selected transition, the extracted ion chromatograms of the individual samples are shown together with the detected peak and its left and right integration borders, so that the integration can be reviewed across the entire analytical sequence at a glance. Moving the pointer over a chromatogram reports the exact retention time at the cursor — the value used when defining fixed peak borders in the transition list (see Input Files — Transition list).

title: MRMhub-viz: Integration Visualizer
text:
The review → refine loop
MRMhub-viz is the inspection half of an iterative loop between visual review and parameter adjustment. Automated integration is rarely optimal for every feature on the first pass; the visualizer identifies where it fails, and the input files are adjusted to correct it. A typical cycle proceeds as follows.

Inspect. Step through the transitions and confirm that the intended peak is detected and correctly bounded, both in the reference samples and across the sequence. Look for missed peaks, co-integrated neighbours, truncated tails, and failures of retention-time tracking.
Diagnose. Relate each problem to the setting responsible for it — a missed peak to RT_tol or RT_shift, a co-integrated neighbour to peak_width, an untracked retention-time jump to RT_shift_bound (see Effects of the key settings).
Refine. Adjust the global parameters in param.txt, or add per-feature overrides in the transition list (peak width, uniform_width, fixed integration bounds) for the problematic minority. Individual peaks that resist automated integration can also have their borders edited directly in RT_matrix.csv.
Re-integrate. After a change to param.txt or the transition list, re-run peak finding (Steps 1–2) followed by integration (Step 3); when only RT_matrix.csv has been edited, re-run Step 3 alone. Reload the dataset in MRMhub-viz and repeat until the integration is satisfactory.







Tip



Refine globally first, then per-feature. Tune param.txt so that the majority of peaks integrate correctly, and reserve transition-list overrides and fixed borders for the remaining difficult peaks. Confirm every change in MRMhub-viz before re-integrating the whole dataset — see the Tuning Peak Integration.








Warning



Re-running Step 2 overwrites RT_matrix.csv. Any manual edits to the integration borders are lost when peak finding is re-run. Make manual RT_matrix.csv adjustments only once the automated integration is otherwise final, then run Step 3 (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 2).

title: Sharing Results & Reproducible Workflows
text: Because INTEGRATOR and MRMhub-viz are self-contained executables that require no installation, a complete peak-integration dataset can be shared as a single folder, allowing others to inspect, reproduce, and modify the raw-data processing. Beyond the CSV tables of peak areas, the raw data, the input files with all integration parameters, and the individual integration results can be bundled together with the applications.

title: Sharing Results & Reproducible Workflows
text:
What to bundle
The components below make a shared dataset fully self-contained. The raw data and input files are what is needed to re-run the processing; the results allow the outcome to be inspected without re-running; and the applications provide the means to do either.

Raw data and input files







Item
Purpose




mzML/ folder
The converted raw data on which integration is performed.


param.txt
All global parameters (tolerances, peak-width windows, RT-shift bounds, threads).


run_order.csv
The sample list, in processing order, with sample/QC types and reference-sample designations.


feature_list.csv
The transitions and features to integrate, including any per-feature overrides.





Results



Item
Purpose




long.csv
The canonical long-format results and the hand-off to the QUANT R package.


quant_raw.csv
The wide-format table of peak areas.


RT_matrix.csv
The finalised integration borders, including any manual adjustments — required to reproduce the exact integration.


misc/ folder
The binary integration results read by MRMhub-viz for interactive review.


PDF folders (optional)
by_transition, by_transition_low, and by_sample PDFs documenting the integration (see Running INTEGRATOR — Step 4).





Applications



Item
Purpose




MRMhub (~1 MB)
The integration application, to re-run or modify any processing step.


MRMhub-viz (~10 MB)
The visualizer, to review the integration interactively (see MRMhub-viz).


MRMhub_plot.r
The base-R script that generates the PDF results; it can be edited to tailor the plot layout.









Tip



Retaining one copy of the applications in each analysis project folder keeps the project reproducible and self-documenting: a recipient can open MRMhub-viz to inspect every peak, or re-run INTEGRATOR to reproduce or adjust the integration, without any installation.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
flow chart for MRMhub INTEGRATOR
Upon execution, the software launches a terminal user interface with four menu options. For new datasets, steps 1 and 2 are applied sequentially. The final step 4 is optional and used only when integration results as PDF files are required.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 1 — Data Validation
The first step verifies the files and information provided in the input files. Inconsistencies are reported in text files saved to the same directory as the MRMhub application. These files are generated only when issues are identified.

missing_files.txt lists mzML files that are present in the data folder but not listed in the Sample List, as well as files listed in the Sample List but absent from the data folder.
missing_compounds.txt reports transitions defined in the Transition List but not found in all mzML files. Note: Transitions present only in a subset of the mzML files are currently not processed.
missing_details.txt details the missing transitions and identifies exactly which samples lack them. This is useful when a transition appears in some samples but not others.







ImportantCurrent limitation — transitions must be present in every mzML file



INTEGRATOR integrates only the transitions common to all mzML files (their intersection) and listed in the transition/feature file. A transition missing from even one mzML file is dropped for the whole dataset, not only for the files that lack it — it is reported in missing_compounds.txt / missing_details.txt. Transitions present in the mzML files but not listed in the feature file are likewise ignored.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
section: Step 2 — Peak Finding and RT-shift estimation
text:
Step 2 — Peak Finding and RT-shift estimation
The second step runs the peak finding and picking algorithm (see Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm for how it works). The result of this step is a table of identified peaks (features) with their left and right peak borders in each sample. This table is saved as the CSV file RT_matrix.csv in the same folder as the application and is required for step 3.
These integration bounds may be refined further on a per-transition and per-sample basis before peak integration is performed in step 3. For a new dataset, the recommended approach is to proceed directly to peak integration, followed by visualization of the results in steps 3 (and 4), and to adjust specific integration borders manually only afterward. Manual adjustment is generally discouraged unless certain integrations can only be achieved through it.
At this point, the integration visualizer application MRMhub-viz (see MRMhub-viz Visualizer) can be launched to inspect the integration results. Global and per-feature integration parameters can then be revised (via param.txt and the Transition List), and peak integration re-attempted via steps 1 and 2.
Once automated integration is considered optimal, final manual adjustments to individual peaks can be made in RT_matrix.csv (see Step 2). After these optional manual adjustments, the final peak integration is performed by (re-)running step 3.
Warning: Each time step 2 is executed, RT_matrix.csv is overwritten and any manual modifications are lost.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 3 — Peak Integration
In the third step, the peaks identified in step 2 are integrated and the corresponding results saved to the following default output files:

quant_raw.csv A wide-format table of peak areas. The top three rows additionally contain the precursor and product m/z and peak apex retention time values.
long.csv A long-format table containing peak area, height, peak apex retention time, FWHM (Full Width at Half Maximum) and integration borders. The corresponding precursor and product m/z values, the analysis time stamp (extracted from the mzML files) and the metadata from the input files (sample type, ISTD, batch identifier) are also included.
misc A folder containing the peak integration results in a binary format, used by the visualizer application MRMhub-viz and in step 4.

All output tables are plain comma-separated CSV files. long.csv is the canonical hand-off to QUANT (one row per sample × feature); quant_raw.csv is a wide-format export of peak areas and is not read by the QUANT module.






Notelong.csv columns





These are the columns QUANT’s import_data_mrmhub() reads from long.csv. Only feature_name and raw_data_filename are strictly required (plus at least one intensity column); the rest are metadata and measurements carried through to the MRMhubExperiment.







long.csv column
Meaning




raw_data_filename
Source mzML file name (becomes the analysis identifier)


time_stamp
Acquisition timestamp, read from the mzML


sample_type
Sample / QC type, from run_order.csv


batch
Batch identifier, from run_order.csv


feature_name
Feature (analyte) identifier, from the transition list


internal_standard
Assigned ISTD feature, from the transition list


rt_apex
Retention time at the peak apex (min)


area
Integrated peak area


height
Peak height


FWHM
Full width at half maximum


rt_int_start / rt_int_end
Left / right integration borders (min)


polarity
Ionisation polarity


precursor_mz / product_mz
Transition m/z values


collision_energy
Collision energy



quant_raw.csv is a wide table of peak areas (features × samples); its top rows additionally carry the precursor and product m/z and the apex retention time per transition.









Tip



Continue post-processing in QUANT. The long.csv file is the canonical hand-off into the QUANT R package: import_data_mrmhub(path = "path/to/long.csv", import_metadata = TRUE) loads the file and its embedded metadata into an MRMhubExperiment for ISTD normalisation, drift/batch correction, QC, and reporting. See the QUANT documentation ↗.

title: Running INTEGRATOR
text:
Step 4 — Generate PDF results (optional)
The fourth step, which is optional, produces integration results as PDF files. It creates three folders with different types of results:

by_transition: Contains one PDF per transition, with chromatograms plotted for each sample. Only transitions with at least one feature (peak) exceeding the minimum intensity threshold value are included here (see by_transition_low).
by_transition_low: Contains PDFs of transitions where none of the integrated features (peaks) had an area exceeding the minimum intensity threshold defined by the constant low_intensity_threshold in the provided MRMhub_plot.r R script.
by_sample: Provides a PDF for each reference sample; all of the sample’s transitions are plotted within the same file.

For efficient viewing of PDFs on macOS, open the PDF folder, press Space to start Quick Look, then use the up/down arrow keys to move between transitions (files). Use the scroll wheel or trackpad to scroll through each PDF.
Note: In large-scale projects, generating many large PDF files can take considerable time, depending on computer performance and the number of cores used. The number of cores used to generate the PDFs can be adjusted via the constant ncores in the provided MRMhub_plot.r script.






Note



Reviewing retention-time stability at scale. The per-transition PDFs provide an efficient means of confirming that RT-shift correction has tracked the peaks across the entire analytical sequence. In a published 4,591-sample lipidomics analysis, for example, RT shifts remained below 0.04 min across the whole run, with the exception of approximately 20 samples at the start of one batch near the end of the sequence, which were readily identified by scanning the by_transition PDFs. See the Dataset 3 workflow ↗.

title: INTEGRATOR
text:
Robust, reproducible peak detection and integration for large-scale targeted LC-MS-MRM analyses




INTEGRATOR is the stand-alone peak-integration module of the MRMhub framework. MS raw data are imported as mzML files, MRMhub is the run as console application in different steps: (1) import and conversion of mzML files, (2) cross-sample peak detection, (3) peak integration, and (4) plotting of chromatograms with integrated peaks as PDFs. Peak area data is saved as long and wide-format CSV files.





 Raw MRM files  mzML (msconvert)  INTEGRATOR   Peak areas long.csv  QUANT ↗


INTEGRATOR performs the peak integration; QUANT (dashed) is a separate MRMhub module.





INTEGRATOR is distributed as a self-contained executable for macOS and Windows via the GitHub releases page; no installation and no separate runtimes are required. A copy of the executable is included in an analysis project, which ensured reproducibility. On first launch, typically a one-time OS security prompt must be cleared. Detailed instructions are given in Installing MRMhub-INTEGRATOR.

Manual — detailed instructions and tool reference is available from the Manual menu above.

The results produced by INTEGRATOR can be used directly by the QUANT R package (mrmhub) for post-processing — normalisation, drift/batch correction, calibration, quality control, and reporting. See the QUANT manual ↗ and the corresponding Demo.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text: This page is a reference for the algorithm that detects, picks, and integrates MRM peaks inside INTEGRATOR. It describes what the software does internally; for the operational menu steps see Running INTEGRATOR, and for how to set each parameter mentioned below see Input Files.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Implementation
INTEGRATOR and its viewer app are implemented as a self-contained, light-weight application for macOS (Apple Silicon) and Windows 11 (x64) that requires no installation. It provides a terminal user interface, while its viewer (MRMhub-viz) comes with a graphical interface.
Considering the scalability to large-scale projects (e.g. > 10,000 samples), INTEGRATOR avoids loading the data from all mzML files into memory simultaneously. Instead, it first surveys peak features across all samples and writes the information to the file system as binary files, which are reloaded as needed in subsequent steps. This design significantly reduces the memory footprint and processing time for large-scale datasets, making it executable on relatively modest hardware — such as a standard laptop.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Sample and transition-list validation
The mzML file names in the sample-list file are checked against the actual files in the data directory provided by the user. Files absent from the directory are reported in a text file (missing_files.txt) so the user can check them. The input transition list is used to assign transition names and attributes to the chromatograms in each mzML file by matching precursor-ion m/z, product-ion m/z, and RT. Transitions that fail to match any chromatogram are skipped and reported in a text file (missing_compounds.txt). Chromatograms in mzML files without any assignment are also excluded from the analysis. The user may proceed with the analysis even if some files or compounds are missing.
A transition is therefore integrated only if it is present in every mzML file and listed in the transition input file: the processed set is the intersection of the transitions common to all files with those defined in the feature list. A transition absent from any single file is currently dropped for the whole dataset, not only for the files that lack it.
Where the same transition (same Q1/Q3 values) with identical or nearly identical MRM start and end windows appears two or more times in an mzML file, the user is alerted and can choose which transition/MRM index to map to which feature in the transition input file.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Retention-time shift correction
The algorithm begins with an initial RT-drift estimation. For each transition, it treats the ion trace in the user-designated reference sample(s) as the reference pattern and uses it to track potential RT drift in all samples. The reference samples are expected to be selected from an early part of the analysis sequence, and not dispersed throughout the entire sequence. The chromatograms in all samples are then aligned to those of the reference samples within individual MRM windows, yielding estimates of the RT shifts.
The user can set a maximum allowance of RT drift (in minutes) in the parameter file (param.txt) using the RT_shift parameter. The syntax is RT_shift = [x, y], where x and y are the forward and backward drift allowances: the algorithm interprets that the RT drift is no more than x minutes earlier and no more than y minutes later than the expected RT in the reference samples. In addition, the RT_shift_bound parameter restricts the RT shift between adjacent sample injections.
RT-shift correction can be disabled by setting RT_shift = [0, 0], which can help for datasets with strong variability of features and/or interferences in the chromatograms, where the cross-correlation approach may yield inaccurate results. In the absence of chromatographic peaks for blank samples, their RT shifts are determined by interpolation from the shifts observed in adjacent samples of the analytical sequence.
When the user chooses to process only a specific part of the chromatograms — by globally setting an RT window relative to the expected RT — RT-shift correction is performed only on the corresponding RT window.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Feature detection
INTEGRATOR performs a first-round search of peak features in all files using continuous wavelet transform (CWT)–based pattern matching. For each MRM window, using the resulting survey of features, the algorithm determines the target number of features per transition as the median number of features detected in the initial survey, and treats it as the upper limit for the number of stable, consistent features to report in the second-round survey.
In the second round, the algorithm maps all peak features across the samples, connecting each peak in one sample to the corresponding peak in the next sample so that every reported feature is stable (i.e. can be detected as a feature) and consistent. The key part of this mapping is that peaks are matched while accounting for the RT drift estimated above. The user sets the RT_tol parameter to indicate the maximum deviation of RT from the value given in the method table. If no feature can be detected within this bound, the integrated area is reported as zero.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Determination of peak integration borders
In the final step, the algorithm goes through the transitions to finalize the integration borders.
For the simple case of unimodal ion traces, the user can set the peak_width parameter quartet [w, x, y, z] to define the default start and end integration points. This can be customized for individual analytes with a peak width column in the transition-list table. The user can also set the uniform_width option (its own column in the transition table) so that the integration width remains the same between samples for a given transition, and can set fixed left/right integration bounds to fix the integration points with respect to the reference samples.
In complex cases — ion traces showing multiple peaks with or without baseline separation — the algorithm searches for valleys between features to cut the integration in the drift-corrected RT space, reconverts the border positions to the original RT space, and writes all RT borders to a CSV file (RT_matrix.csv) for user inspection and optional manual adjustment before peak areas are calculated.

title: Peak Detection and Integration Algorithm
text:
Baseline determination
The baseline is determined on the x axis from the integration borders. On the y axis, three modes are available:

5th percentile (default) — a horizontal baseline set at the 5th percentile of the intensities within the integration window.
v_drop — a horizontal baseline set at the lowest intensity of the integrated region.
Valley-to-valley — a sloped baseline fitted between the points where the left and right integration borders intersect the ion trace.







Note



Where to set these parameters. RT_shift, RT_shift_bound, RT_tol, peak_width, uniform_width, and the fixed integration bounds are all configured in param.txt and the transition list — see Input Files for the syntax and defaults, and Tuning Peak Integration for choosing values. To see the algorithm in action across the four processing steps, see Running INTEGRATOR.

title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
text: This page collects frequent questions and failure modes. For the input-file reference see Input Files, for choosing parameter values see Tuning Peak Integration, and for the processing steps see Running INTEGRATOR.

title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
text:
Preparing the input files

A CSV file is misread — columns look shifted or values are wrong
run_order.csv and feature_list.csv are read by column position, not by header name, so a reordered, deleted, or inserted column is silently misinterpreted. Restore the template column order (see Input Files). Beyond column order, run_order.csv and feature_list.csv are plain, comma-separated, UTF-8 files that spreadsheet editors corrupt silently:

Auto-conversion — leading zeros are dropped and values such as 16:0 or 1-2 are coerced to dates or times. Format the affected cells as text, or edit in a plain-text editor.
Delimiter / locale — the separator must be a comma. Locales that default to a semicolon (;) produce a single-column file that is misread.
Encoding — save as UTF-8 without a byte-order mark (BOM); a BOM corrupts the first header.
Stray whitespace and blank rows — trailing spaces in identifiers and empty trailing rows are read as data.
File names — the file name entries must match the mzML files exactly, including the .mzML extension and case.



Which input files are required, and can they be renamed?
param.txt must be named param.txt and reside in the same folder as the executable. The sample list and transition/feature list may take any name, set by batch_info and transition_list in param.txt (defaults run_order.csv and feature_list.csv). See Input Files.

title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
text:
Validation and matching (Step 1)

What do missing_files.txt, missing_compounds.txt, and missing_details.txt mean?
These are written by Step 1 (Data Validation) only when problems are found:

missing_files.txt — mzML files listed in the sample list but absent from the data folder, or present in the folder but not listed.
missing_compounds.txt — transitions defined in the transition list but not matched in the mzML files.
missing_details.txt — which samples lack a given transition (useful when a transition is present in only some files).

The analysis may proceed with items missing. See Running INTEGRATOR — Step 1.


A transition is not matched
Matching is by precursor m/z, product m/z, and RT, within mz_tol and RT_tol. Confirm the transition-list values against the mzML, and widen mz_tol if the instrument’s m/z calibration is slightly off.


Why was a transition dropped from every sample?
Current limitation. INTEGRATOR integrates only the transitions common to all mzML files (their intersection) and listed in the transition/feature file. A transition missing from even one mzML file is dropped for the whole dataset — not only for the files that lack it — and reported in missing_compounds.txt / missing_details.txt. Ensure the transition is acquired in every sample, or exclude the files/features that do not share it. See Running INTEGRATOR — Step 1.


The same transition appears more than once in an mzML file
Where a transition with identical (or near-identical) Q1/Q3 and MRM windows occurs multiple times, INTEGRATOR prompts for which MRM index to map to the feature; the chromatogram index column in the transition list can also fix the assignment.

title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
text:
Peak detection and integration

A feature’s area is reported as zero
No peak was detected within RT_tol of the expected RT. Check the expected RT in the transition list, confirm the precursor/product m/z match within mz_tol, and, for genuinely drifting peaks, widen RT_tol. See Tuning Peak Integration.


A wrong, co-eluting, or adjacent peak is integrated
Usually RT_tol or peak_width is too wide, or the expected RT is off. Narrow the window, or set a per-feature peak width or fixed integration bounds for the affected feature. Confirm every change in MRMhub-viz before re-integrating. See Tuning Peak Integration.


Retention-time drift is not tracked across the sequence
Reference samples must be chosen from early in the sequence and be mutually well aligned, and RT_shift / RT_shift_bound must accommodate the real drift. See Peak-detection algorithm and Tuning Peak Integration.


I edited an input file — what must be re-run?
Editing any input file requires restarting from Step 1. Editing only RT_matrix.csv (manual border adjustments) requires re-running Step 3 alone — re-running Step 2 overwrites RT_matrix.csv. See Running INTEGRATOR.

title: FAQ & Troubleshooting
text:
Running the application

The application will not open (macOS “cannot be verified” / Windows “blocked”)
The executables are unsigned, so the operating system shows a one-time security prompt on first launch. See clearing the first-launch security prompt.

title: Quick Start
text: This short tutorial presents the steps to create a basic peak integration project. Input files are prepared, the integration run, and result inspected and integration refined.

title: Quick Start
section: 1. Convert the raw files to mzML
text:
1. Convert the raw files to mzML
INTEGRATOR requires MS raw data in the open mzML format. Native vendor files (e.g. Thermo .raw, SCIEX .wiff, Agilent .d) must first be converted with ProteoWizard MSConvert (Windows only), which needs to be done only once per dataset → mzML conversion.

title: Quick Start
text:
2. Set up the project
A project is a single, self-contained folder holding the executable, input files, raw data, and results, keeping the full analysis and dataset transferable and reproducible. Assemble it as follows; see Installing MRMhub-INTEGRATOR for obtaining INTEGRATOR, the first-launch security prompt, and the full project layout.

Create the project folder and move the .mzML files into a subfolder (e.g., mzML/).
Add the INTEGRATOR tools — the executables and the plotting script, from a release or an existing project.
Add the input templates — from a release or the templates folder.


my-project/
├── MRMhub.exe / .app      ← peak-integration executable
├── MRMhub-viz.exe / .app  ← visualiser (optional)
├── MRMhub_plot.r          ← R script for creating chromatogram PDFs
├── mzML/                  ← the .mzML files
├── param.txt          ┐
├── run_order.csv      ├  input templates (step 3)
└── feature_list.csv   ┘
Project folder layout prior to integration

title: Quick Start
text:
3. Prepare the input files
Edit and review the input files that configure the peak integration run, one global, and two defining the samples and the features. See the Input Files reference for description of all parameters.




File
Configuration




param.txt
Name and location of the input and mzML files, the global peak-detection and border-finding settings, and the RT-shift correction parameters. Must be in the same folder as the MRMhub executable.


run_order.csv
The mzML files to process, listed in run order, optionally, the reference sample(s) for RT-shift estimation. sample_type is optional, with only blanks (BLK) being treated specially


feature_list.csv
Transition precursor and product m/z values, transition and feature identifiers, the expected feature RT, optional per-feature integration settings.

title: Quick Start
text:
4. Run INTEGRATOR
INTEGRATOR is launched from the project folder and its terminal menu is worked through in order; see Running INTEGRATOR for the full reference. It is started by double-clicking MRMhub (macOS) or MRMhub.exe (Windows), or from a terminal opened in the project folder.



The INTEGRATOR terminal menu.



Data Validation — the input files are loaded and checked for inconsistencies (mzML files or transitions that are listed but missing, or present but unlisted). Report files are written only if problems are found (see file tree below)
Peak Finding & RT-shift estimation — peaks are detected and the retention-time shift across the sequence is estimated. Produces RT_matrix.csv (the detected peaks with their per-sample integration borders), which is required for step 3.
Peak Integration — the peaks from step 2 are integrated. Produces long.csv (the canonical hand-off to QUANT), quant_raw.csv (wide-format peak areas), and the misc/ folder (binary results used by MRMhub-viz and step 4).
Generate PDF results (optional) — the integrated chromatograms are plotted as PDFs, grouped into by_transition/, by_transition_low/, and by_sample/.

The steps run in order, each using the previous one’s output (steps 1–3 for a new dataset; step 4 optional). The application can be closed and reopened between steps — intermediate files persist, so the run can be resumed. Editing any input file, however, requires restarting from step 1. The run adds these outputs to the project folder:

my-project/
├── missing_files.txt     ┐
├── missing_compounds.txt ├ step 1: validation reports (only if problems found)
├── missing_details.txt   ┘
├── RT_matrix.csv         ← step 2: peaks + per-sample borders
├── long.csv              ← step 3: long-format integration results table 
├── quant_raw.csv         ← step 3: wide-format peak areas
├── misc/                 ← step 3: binary results (used for MRMhub-viz)
├── by_transition/        ┐
├── by_transition_low/    ├ step 4 (optional): chromatogram PDFs
├── by_sample/            ┘
└── …                     ← executable, mzML/, input files (unchanged)
Files and folders added by the run, each annotated with the step that creates it







Important



On first launch after download the operating system shows a one-time security prompt (macOS Gatekeeper / Windows “Unblock”). See clearing the security prompt.

title: Quick Start
text:
5. Review the results
The chromatograms and peak integration results can be reviewed in either of two ways:

From the PDFs (if step 4 was run) — the per-transition and per-sample PDFs can be browsed quickly with a file previewer: macOS Quick Look (press Space) or the Windows File Explorer preview pane, switching transitions with the arrow keys and scrolling with the mouse wheel.
Interactively in the MRMhub-viz app — results are examined feature by feature. → MRMhub-viz

Guided by the review, the global and per-feature settings can be refined and INTEGRATOR re-run, until the integration is satisfactory across the sequence. Individual peak boundaries can also be corrected per sample by editing RT_matrix.csv and re-running only step 3 — re-running step 2 overwrites these manual edits.

title: Quick Start
text:
6. Integration results
INTEGRATOR writes the integration results as different tables to the project folder:

quant_raw.csv (wide format) — a features × samples matrix of peak areas only, with the precursor and product m/z and the median apex RT carried in the top rows.
long.csv (long format) — one row per sample × feature, with area, height, FWHM, and apex RT , and transition m/z, acquisition timestamp, and metadata from the input files.
RT_matrix.csv — the peak boundaries per feature and sample, produced in step 2. These can be edited to adjust individual peaks (see Review the results).

See Running INTEGRATOR for the full definition of these file formats.

title: Quick Start
text:
7. Post-processing
One recommended route is MRMhub QUANT, the postprocessing module of MRMhub. An R package offering functions, which imports INTEGRATOR’s long.csv directly for normalisation, drift and batch correction, calibration, quality control, and reporting:
mrmhub::import_data_mrmhub(path = "path/to/long.csv", import_metadata = TRUE)
→ QUANT Quick Start ↗ · QUANT documentation ↗

title: Installation
text: INTEGRATOR is a self-contained, portable executable and requires no installer: the application is downloaded, unzipped, and run from a folder, with one copy kept per analysis project (see below).

title: Installation
text:
System requirements
Pre-compiled binaries are provided for macOS (Apple silicon), Windows 11 (x86-64), and Linux (x86-64). A multi-core CPU is recommended, as the integration is parallelised. Memory requirements are 8 GB minimum, 16 GB recommended for large projects. The application itself occupies minimal disk space, but the integration outputs — internal files (the misc/ folder), result tables, and generated PDFs — can require considerable space depending on dataset size.
INTEGRATOR itself has no runtime dependencies. The following external tools may be required:

mzML conversion — ProteoWizard MSConvert (Windows only), see mzML conversion.
PDF chromatogram plotting — an R installation. Download the installer from CRAN; no additional R packages are required.

title: Installation
text:
Download
Pre-compiled executables for macOS, Windows, and Linux are available from the GitHub releases page. The archive contains the executables — MRMhub (MRMhub-INTEGRATOR) and MRMhub-viz (integration viewer app), the MRMhub_plot.r R script, template input files (param.txt, run_order.csv, feature_list.csv), and a complete test dataset.

title: Installation
text:
Clearing the first-launch security prompt






Important



The executables are unsigned, so a security prompt appears on first launch — on macOS the developer “cannot be verified”, on Windows the file is “blocked”. This does not indicate an issue with the software.


To clear the security block, the following must be done for each downloaded executable:

macOS (left) — System Settings → Privacy & Security → click Open Anyway.
Windows (right) — right-click executable → Properties → tick Unblock (if present) → OK.

title: Installation
text:
Verify the installation
Every release bundles a demonstration dataset with input files that runs end-to-end without further preparation — the quickest confirmation that the installation works. See Demo.

title: Installation
section: Setting up a peak integration project
text:
Setting up a peak integration project
The unzipped folder can serve directly as a peak-integration project — a self-contained folder holding the executables, the input files, and the raw data. The mzML files are placed in a subfolder (e.g. mzML/, as specified in param.txt). The three input files (param.txt, run_order.csv, feature_list.csv) must be edited to the specific dataset — its samples, features, and integration settings — as described in Input Files. The integration is then run within this folder — see Running INTEGRATOR for the processing steps.

my-project/
├── MRMhub.exe / .app      ← peak-integration executable
├── MRMhub-viz.exe / .app  ← results visualiser (optional)
├── MRMhub_plot.r          ← R script for chromatogram PDFs (optional step 4)
├── param.txt          ┐
├── run_order.csv      ├  input files (see Input Files)
├── feature_list.csv   ┘
└── mzML/                  ← the converted .mzML data files
A project folder assembled and ready to run. Files added by a run are documented in Running INTEGRATOR.








TipKeep one INTEGRATOR copy per project



A separate copy of INTEGRATOR is kept in each project, with its data and input files, so the analysis stays reproducible and transferable. As parameters and input-file formats may change between versions, keeping the executable with the project also ensures the input files match the version that produced the results.

title: Installation
text:
Updating INTEGRATOR
To update INTEGRATOR, replace the executables in the project folder with a newer release. New versions are mostly backward-compatible, but may occasionally require adapting the input files, as new functionality may add or change parameters.

title: Tuning Peak Integration
text: The parameters defined in param.txt and the transition/feature list govern how INTEGRATOR detects and bounds peaks. This page describes how each setting behaves and how to choose values for difficult chromatograms. For the field-by-field syntax and defaults see Input Files; for the underlying method see the Algorithm. Confirm the effect of any change visually in MRMhub-viz before re-integrating the whole dataset.

title: Tuning Peak Integration
text:
Effects of the key settings
Most settings trade sensitivity (finding and fully capturing the intended peak) against specificity (not grabbing a neighbouring transition, an adjacent peak, or noise). The table summarises the behaviour at each extreme; peak_width, the most influential setting for difficult chromatograms, is detailed below.









Setting
What it controls
Too small/narrow
Too large/wide




mz_tol
How far the detected m/z may deviate from the transition-list value
A transition may not be matched at all if the instrument’s m/z calibration is slightly off
A nearby transition / channel may be matched by mistake


RT_tol
The retention-time window searched around the expected RT (key for complex chromatograms)
The peak is missed when its RT drifts beyond the window
A wrong, co-eluting, or adjacent peak may be selected instead of the intended one


peak_width [w,x,y,z]
Allowed windows for the left (w–x) and right (y–z) peak borders, relative to the apex
Incomplete integration — tailing or broadened peaks are cut short
Smaller adjacent/interfering peaks are co-integrated into the area


RT_shift [x,y]
The maximum RT drift expected across the reference samples
Genuine drift between references is not accommodated, degrading peak tracking
The search window is unnecessarily wide, raising the chance of picking the wrong peak


RT_shift_bound
The maximum RT drift allowed between adjacent samples
A real run-to-run RT jump can break sample-to-sample tracking
Spurious jumps may be followed, tracking drift that is not present


num_threads
CPU threads used for integration
Slower processing only — no effect on results
Faster, bounded by available cores — no effect on results









Tip



Set the parameters globally in param.txt to suit the majority of peaks, then apply per-feature overrides in the transition list (peak width, uniform_width, fixed integration bounds) to the problematic minority only.








Tip



Worked example. A published lipidomics dataset (Agilent triple-quadrupole) used mz_tol = 0.06, RT_tol = 0.04, and peak_width = [0.15, 0.08, 0.08, 0.18] globally, with per-feature overrides for broad or convoluted peaks, an RT-shift window of (-0.1, 0.4), and a maximum sample-to-sample RT shift (RT_shift_bound) of 0.05. These are reasonable starting points for a fast, well-resolved method. See the full Dataset 3 workflow ↗ for the complete input files and the resulting integration.

title: Tuning Peak Integration
section: Setting the peak-width and integration bounds
text:
Setting the peak-width and integration bounds
The peak_width parameter — global in param.txt, optionally overridden per feature in the transition list — is the key setting for automated integration of complex chromatograms. It is specified as [w, x, y, z], where the ranges w–x and y–z define the allowed windows for the left and right peak borders, respectively. The algorithm constrains the peak start and end points to these ranges, even where automatic boundary detection would otherwise extend beyond them.
Ranges that are too narrow yield incomplete integration, particularly for tailing peaks or peaks of unstable width; ranges that are too wide cause smaller adjacent peaks to be co-integrated. A global setting suited to the majority of peaks is defined in param.txt, with per-feature settings applied to convoluted, asymmetric, or broadened peaks. Narrower per-feature ranges are also used where nearby interferences are not recognised as separate peaks and are consequently co-integrated.








Examples of manually set peak boundaries in INTEGRATOR. (a, b) Effect of the peak_width parameter on a peak with clear tailing (PC 36:6): (a) the global setting, suitable for the majority of peaks, and (b) a feature-specific peak width overriding the global value for improved integration. (c, d) Effect on a peak with nearby interferences (PC O-38:4): (c) the global setting, and (d) an excessively wide peak_width that causes incorrect integration, underscoring the importance of an appropriate global value. (e, f) A complex chromatogram of three overlapping LPC 17:0 isomers: (e) the global setting yields only partial integration, with the first peak unrecognised, whereas (f) fixed boundaries defined for the first peak enable correct picking and integration of all three isomers.


Set uniform_width to y for features whose integration is correct in most samples but inaccurate in a minority: the integration width is then held constant across samples for that transition.
Use fixed left/right integration bounds where automated integration, even after tuning peak_width, does not consistently integrate convoluted peaks or peaks with nearby interferences. Fixed borders are a last resort, since they may require re-adjustment when the same method is applied to other datasets. These borders are still adjusted for retention-time shifts.
